planting.note: Set out after the soil has warmed in a site with sharp drainage, since this compact butterfly bush resents soggy roots over winter.

directions: Grow this dwarf reworking of the original Pugster White in full sun with well-drained soil, where it forms a dense mound topped with large white flower spikes from summer into fall. Unlike the earlier release, the blooms hold a clean white tone instead of fading to a muddy yellow-brown as they age. No deadheading is required to keep flowers coming, and the compact habit suits both border plantings and large containers. It tolerates heat well and shows good resistance to common butterfly bush diseases.

planting.note: Install in neutral to alkaline, well-drained soil and top with about an inch of mulch to protect shallow roots.

directions: This evergreen boxwood from the disease-screened NewGen breeding program holds bright, clear variegated foliage year-round without the bronzing many boxwoods show in winter. It was selected for improved tolerance of boxwood blight and boxwood leafminer, making it a sturdier option for hedges, borders, and foundation plantings. It accepts full sun to shade, giving it more placement flexibility than many broadleaf evergreens. Plant in neutral to alkaline soil with reliable drainage for the densest, healthiest growth.

planting.note: Plant into clay-tolerant garden soil; cut stems back by about a third in early spring as new growth begins since flowers form on new wood.

directions: A newer entry in the Invincibelle breeding line of native smooth hydrangea, this selection carries unusually sturdy stems that hold up deep pink, deeply ribbed flower heads without flopping. It reblooms through the season, giving continuous color from summer into fall, and the sturdy stems make it a good candidate for cutting. It tolerates road salt and clay soils better than many hydrangeas, and because color is set genetically rather than by soil pH, blooms stay reliably pink regardless of soil chemistry.

planting.note: Set in average garden soil and prune back by roughly a third in early spring, since bloom forms on the current season's new growth.

directions: This smooth hydrangea opens deep red-pink blooms that shift toward a near-purple hue as they mature, giving a two-tone effect across the flower head. Sturdy stems support the mophead blooms through summer and into fall without staking, and the plant reblooms readily on new growth. It works equally well as a foundation shrub, a cut-flower source, or a pollinator-friendly border plant, and unlike bigleaf hydrangeas its color is not altered by soil pH.

planting.note: Give at least 6 hours of direct sun, with afternoon shade appreciated in hot-summer regions; tolerates clay soil.

directions: A semi-dwarf addition to the Invincibelle series of native smooth hydrangea, this selection produces full, rounded mophead blooms in a clean, powder-puff pink on compact, well-branched plants. Strong stems keep the flower heads upright through summer rain and wind, and the shrub reblooms on new wood through the season. Its smaller stature fits tighter garden spaces than the full-size Invincibelle cultivars while retaining the reliable rebloom and clay-soil tolerance the series is known for.

planting.note: Choose a sheltered site with reliably drained soil; this species is hardier than its tropical look suggests but still benefits from winter protection at the colder end of its range.

directions: Native to Chinese mountain forests, this velvet hydrangea carries large, deep purple, fuzzy-textured leaves that give it an almost tropical presence despite surprising cold hardiness. Lacecap flower heads combine pink sterile florets with purple-blue fertile centers in summer, followed by good fall foliage interest. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape, and site it in a border, foundation planting, or naturalized area with full sun to part sun. It tolerates heat well for a species of this type, broadening where it can be grown successfully.
